intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that myofibrillar myopathy-1 (MFM1), also known as desmin-related myopathy, is caused by heterozygous, homozygous, or compound heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding desmin (DES) on chromosome 2q35.

paragraphs.text: Desmin-related myopathy is a familial disorder characterized by skeletal muscle weakness associated with cardiac conduction blocks, arrhythmias, and restrictive heart failure, and by intracytoplasmic accumulation of desmin-reactive deposits in cardiac and skeletal muscle cells (Goldfarb et al., 1998). van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al. (2011) described it as an autosomally inherited skeletal and cardiac myopathy mainly caused by dominant mutations in the DES gene; Pinol-Ripoll et al. (2009) noted that autosomal recessive mutations are rare. Selcen et al. (2004) stated that the term myofibrillar myopathy (MFM) was proposed in 1996 as a noncommittal term for a pathologic pattern of myofibrillar dissolution with accumulation of myofibrillar degradation products and ectopic expression of multiple proteins, and that MFM is morphologically distinct but genetically heterogeneous.

paragraphs.text: Messina et al. (1997) designated the disorder they linked to chromosome 6q23 as familial dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction defect and muscular dystrophy (FDC-CDM). paragraphs.text: Porte et al. (1980) reported 3 brothers with progressive myocardial deficiency. Cardiac muscle cells showed massive storage of PAS-negative proteinaceous material, which by electron microscopy consisted of sinuous filaments 7 to 10 nm in diameter, similar to intermediate filaments. Filament storage coincided with disintegration of neighboring myofibrils, with Z-band changes giving rise to rod-like bodies. Filament deposits were also observed in a few skeletal muscle fibers. The authors suggested that a disturbance in the metabolism of desmin might be involved.

paragraphs.text: Abe et al. (1993) described a Japanese kindred with an autosomal dominant progressive myopathy with diffuse cytoplasmic bodies. Twelve patients in 4 successive generations had weakness and atrophy of muscles of the distal extremities, neck, thorax, and shoulder girdles. Mean age at onset was 42 years, and patients became disabled after 5 to 10 years due to chronic respiratory failure. Serum creatine kinase was normal or slightly elevated, and EMG showed predominantly myopathic changes with slight neurogenic change. Autopsy of 2 cases showed numerous cytoplasmic bodies, predominantly in type I fibers, and smooth and cardiac muscles were also affected. Males were affected more frequently than females (2:1).

Twelve patients had myopathy, with weakness that was axial in mildly affected, axial and predominantly distal in moderately affected, and generalized in severely affected patients. paragraphs.text: Pinol-Ripoll et al. (2009) reported a girl, the only child of consanguineous (uncle-niece) parents, who had recurrent syncope from 6 months of age, initially attributed to Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. At age 15 years she had bilateral facial weakness, ptosis, symmetric scapular winging, atrophy of masseter, temporalis, sternocleidomastoid, and trunk muscles, pes cavus, and mild weakness of the shoulder girdle and distal muscles. Creatine kinase was twice normal, and EMG showed complex repetitive discharges, some myotonic discharges, and a myopathic recruitment pattern. Holter monitoring showed ventricular tachycardia, QT prolongation, and second-degree AV block, and a defibrillator and pacemaker were implanted. At age 18 years she had episodes of ventricular tachyarrhythmia, and echocardiography indicated restrictive cardiomyopathy. Diarrhea, vomiting, and weight loss suggested intestinal smooth muscle involvement, and she died from cardiac failure before her 21st birthday. More than 90% of muscle fibers contained subsarcolemmal desmin-immunoreactive, Congo red-positive deposits, and electron microscopy showed granulofilamentous material.

paragraphs.text: In a meta-analysis of 159 DES mutation carriers with 40 different mutations, van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so the intro gives no MIM number for the DES gene; I took its location (2q35) from the papers. Bushby and Beckmann 2003, Straub 2018 (LGMD nomenclature; the title alone does not support the LGMD2R reclassification) and Barohn 1998 (a general overview of distal myopathies) are not cited. The abstracts give no nucleotide changes for most early mutations, and no exact name for the deep intronic variant in Riley et al. (2019). The Bar et al. (2007) tail mutations T442I and S460I are not listed as allelic variants because the abstract does not describe the patients who carry them.
